analysis.title: The Yield Curve Has A Nasty Surprise For The AI Trade
key_insights: Semiconductors are the sector most exposed to a yield-curve flattening driven by tighter liquidity. They are also the most crowded sector, so they are most vulnerable to a politically driven change in sentiment toward data-center construction.

Excess liquidity (real M1 growth minus economic growth) has declined for over three months, and its impact is only now being felt. Its turns typically lead turns in the yield curve by 6-9 months, with exceptions in the 2010s QE years.
Yesterday's Treasury quarterly funding announcement hinted at less long-end issuance. The author says this does no harm to excess liquidity's prediction of a flatter curve.
Stocks are underperforming bonds and the 3m-10y curve has flattened more than 40 bps since early October. The author reads this as the liquidity squeeze showing up in markets.
Semis are the sector most positively sensitive to the yield curve, followed by energy. A flattening therefore hurts semis most, though the sensitivity is relatively small.

A flatter curve should keep favoring smaller-cap S&P 500 stocks, so the S&P equal-weight index should keep outperforming the cap-weighted index. The equal-weight index's correlation to the curve is more negative and decaying faster, which implies relative underperformance for the hyper-caps.

Semis and energy are both highly cyclical. Semis track new orders in the manufacturing ISM closely. The author is skeptical of the argument that AI compute demand has made semis immune to the cycle, since it rests on untested beliefs that compute intensity and AI demand are unbounded.

Semis have the third-highest Hype Score (forward earnings, institutional ownership, analyst ratings, short interest), just behind capital goods and utilities. Semis are still crowded despite a 30% drawdown. Post-midterm fears over data-center approvals could trigger an exit by the crowd while the curve flattens.
Software's Hype Score surged and then fell earlier this year when it became an anti-AI trade. Software has recovered most of its losses but is not crowded, so its returns are less exposed.

Real estate and consumer durables are the two most uncrowded sectors and the most negatively correlated to the yield curve. The author says they stand to benefit most from a flatter curve while being contrarian.

tension_points.bull_case: Accelerated computing demand from data centers has made the sector immune to the cycle, with AI demand essentially unbounded.
tension_points.bear_case: This rests on untested beliefs. The sector still tracks manufacturing ISM new orders, and its stocks can be cyclical even if the industry is not.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A flatter yield curve and a turning cycle will test the immunity claim: the author says "we'll soon find out" as the cycle turns and the curve flattens.
